case_study_insert.main_stem: Ridgeview Timber Products (RTPL) is a worker cooperative in the sustainable construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2008 by Tomas Berg, the business supplies reclaimed timber flooring to decorators and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. RTPL plans to invest $640,000 in a reclaimed-timber grading and drying line, financed by a $240,000 bank loan and $400,000 from a share issue of member shares. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. RTPL faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and timber waste is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The reclaimed-timber line processed 19,000 board metres last quarter at a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 5.0% a year ago. Customer complaints about warped boards fell from 31 to 14 per month. Average delivery lead time is 6.2 days. Timber waste is currently 8.8% of input. A survey of 350 decorators found that 62% would pay $0.75 more for certified reclaimed flooring, and 49% check sustainability labels before ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 36 operatives have not completed on-the-job training on the new grading saw; off-the-job courses at the training centre cost $620 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ridgeview Timber Products for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, raising debt-service costs for variable-rate borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% from $12.60 to $13.20 an hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills. (3) Wholesale timber and transport input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, while construction-material inflation is 5.9% and spending on home renovation grew 3.1%.

questions.question_text: RTPL plans to fund its $640,000 grading and drying line partly with a $240,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for RTPL of raising the $400,000 balance through a share issue rather than more borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Member share capital does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, so RTPL avoids adding debt service to its $280,000 fixed costs while labour turnover of 14% already disrupts the 80,000-unit output. The $240,000 bank loan can then be serviced from contribution of $8.00 a unit without the extra burden of a second loan.

Point 2: Issuing member shares strengthens the cooperative's own capital base and keeps ownership with the 36 worker-members, supporting the laissez-faire culture and long-term commitment. A bank would require security and covenants over the new grading saw; member equity has no such conditions, so the 11.2% rise in timber and transport costs can be absorbed without breaching lending terms or risking the reclaimed-timber line.

Because the cooperative already has a $240,000 loan, keeping the new capital as member equity avoids pushing interest costs higher and preserves the improving gross margin trend in Appendix 2 while the grading line beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of share issue finance over debt (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to RTPL's cooperative structure and expansion.

questions.question_text: RTPL wants to grow sales of its certified reclaimed flooring. Consider selling only through decorators' merchants, launching an e-commerce website, or supplying national DIY chains. Which should RTPL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Decorators' merchants only: This keeps distribution simple and uses existing relationships with the 350 decorators surveyed, giving predictable orders and low selling costs for a cooperative of 36. It caps reach, however: relying on one channel leaves RTPL exposed if merchants cut stock, and the 62% who would pay $0.75 more may never see the product, wasting the $640,000 grading-line investment.

E-commerce website: An online shop can display certification and sustainability labels directly to the 49% of decorators who check them, take orders nationally and build a customer database for repeat sales, at a modest setup cost beside a $640,000 line. It needs delivery logistics for heavy flooring, returns management and digital marketing skills that a 36-member cooperative may lack, and transport costs are already up 11.2%.

National DIY chains: Supplying chains would deliver very high volume and fill the 80,000-unit capacity quickly, but margins would be squeezed by the chain's buying power, threatening the $20.00 price and $8.00 contribution. Listing fees and strict delivery schedules would strain the 6.2-day lead time and the 14% labour turnover.

Recommendation: RTPL should launch an e-commerce website, retaining merchant sales as a base. E-commerce reaches the sustainability-minded segment in the 350-decorator survey without surrendering margin to DIY chains, and it can be built with the $400,000 member share capital. Merchants-only is rejected as too narrow for the new capacity; DIY chains are rejected because their price pressure and delivery demands would undermine the $8.00 contribution and the cooperative's quality positioning.

It can also be expanded gradually as the line reaches 80,000 units.

level_1_1_to_4: Limited awareness of the three distribution options with minimal RTPL context.
level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to RTPL's survey and costs.
level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why merchants-only and DIY chains are rejected.

questions.question_text: RTPL's labour turnover has reached 14%. Explain two ways financial motivators could help reduce it.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A performance-related bonus tied to the 3.4% defect rate and on-time delivery would give the 36 worker-members a direct financial stake in quality, raising effort and reducing the 8.8% timber waste. Because the bonus is paid only when targets are met, it links pay to the $20.00 selling price and $8.00 contribution rather than adding a fixed cost like the $280,000 overhead.

Point 2: Profit sharing distributes part of RTPL's gains across all members, reinforcing the cooperative's ownership culture and discouraging workers from leaving for higher wages elsewhere; with labour turnover at 14%, the $620-per-person off-the-job course cost is avoided when staff stay. Shared reward also supports laissez-faire leadership, as members monitor each other's output of 80,000 units without close supervision.

Both motivators can be introduced without changing the $20.00 price, and the cooperative can link rewards to the 3.4% defect rate and 6.2-day delivery time so effort is measurable rather than symbolic.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid financial motivator and its effect (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to RTPL's turnover, waste and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: Labour turnover at RTPL has reached 14%. Consider recruiting experienced graders externally or training existing operatives. Which should RTPL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment: Hiring experienced graders could bring immediate skill to the new grading saw, reduce the 3.4% defect rate quickly and inject fresh ideas into a cooperative where 14% of staff have already left. Advertising, selection and induction cost money and time, and new starters may not fit the laissez-faire, member-owned culture; with the $240,000 loan to service, a costly recruitment round is risky, and 14 of 36 operatives still need training whatever happens.

Training existing operatives: Off-the-job courses at $620 per person would cost $8,680 for the 14 operatives (14 x $620), small beside the $640,000 line, and on-the-job coaching on the grading saw is specific to RTPL's reclaimed timber. Training retains cooperative knowledge, improves commitment and addresses the 14% turnover directly. It takes time to lift productivity, and trained members could still leave, but the cost is far below repeated recruitment.

Decision: RTPL should train existing operatives, with targeted external hiring only for a supervisor if no member has the skill. Internal training is cheaper, protects the $8.00 contribution from recruitment fees and directly counters 14% turnover by investing in the 36 members. External recruitment is rejected because induction costs and cultural fit risks are high, and hiring strangers while 14 of 36 staff remain untrained would weaken commitment to the worker cooperative.

Training also protects the cooperative's specific knowledge of reclaimed-timber grading, which would be lost if skilled members left. RTPL can measure success through the 3.4% defect rate and 14% turnover figures over the next two quarters before reconsidering external hires.

level_1_1_to_4: Basic comparison of internal and external recruitment with limited RTPL application.
level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of costs, speed and cultural fit of both options using RTPL's audit and turnover figures.
level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision referencing cost, turnover and cooperative culture.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RTPL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $12.00) = $280,000 ÷ $8.00 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $12.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways the management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 35,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 45,000 units, so the cooperative can judge how much sales may fall before losses occur while labour turnover is 14%.
2. Use the $8.00 contribution to test the survey finding that 62% would pay $0.75 more: a $0.75 premium would lift contribution to $8.75, showing the reward from pursuing certified reclaimed flooring.
3. Translate the 35,000-unit break-even point into a loan-service target for the $240,000 bank loan, confirming the $640,000 drying line can be paid for from operations before committing member share capital further.
4. Monitor average total cost of $15.50 a unit ($280,000 ÷ 80,000 = $3.50 plus $12.00) against the 8.8% timber waste, so managers can detect whether waste reduction is protecting margins as 11.2% input inflation bites.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 45,000 units against 80,000 output; modelling the $0.75 premium on $8.00 contribution; loan-service volume for the $240,000 loan; and average total cost benchmarking at $15.50 to monitor 8.8% waste and 11.2% inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RTPL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Has RTPL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 34.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 9.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of 600 on revenue of 2,000 gives 30.0% in 2024, and 850 on 2,500 gives 34.0% in 2025. Operating profit of 180 on revenue of 2,000 gives 9.0%, and 300 on 2,500 gives 12.0%. Operating profit of 180 on capital employed of 1,200 gives 15.0%, and 300 on 1,500 gives 20.0%. Revenue increased by 500 while cost of sales increased by 250, and interest payable rose from 24 to 30.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The 30.0% to 34.0% gross margin indicates better control of reclaimed-timber input costs relative to sales, important given the $12.00 variable cost and 8.8% waste. The 9.0% to 12.0% operating margin shows overheads were absorbed as revenue grew, since operating profit rose by 120. The 15.0% to 20.0% return on capital employed is the strongest signal: despite member share capital and the $240,000 loan widening the capital base from 1,200 to 1,500, operating profit still rose fast enough to raise returns. Interest payable increased from 24 to 30, a small drag, but not enough to reverse the trend.

Conclusion: RTPL's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose together, so the gain is not just higher sales. The main caution is the higher interest charge attached to the $240,000 loan, yet the cooperative's investment in the $640,000 line appears justified so far.

level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures from Appendix 2 without accurate ratio calculation.
level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three measures for both years accurately and describes the trend with some RTPL context.
level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RTPL of using certified reclaimed timber.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certification supports the 62% of 350 surveyed decorators who would pay $0.75 more and the 49% who check sustainability labels, protecting the $20.00 price and $8.00 contribution despite an 11.2% rise in timber and transport costs. It also differentiates the cooperative when bidding for renovation work, which grew 3.1%, helping utilise the $640,000 grading line.

Disadvantage: Verifying and grading reclaimed timber adds handling and inspection, which can lift the $12.00 variable cost and may worsen the 3.4% defect rate and 8.8% waste if inconsistent timber is accepted. Certification audits take member time away from the 80,000-unit output target, and if the $0.75 premium is not realised in practice, RTPL bears the cost without extra revenue, squeezing the cooperative's returns.

The cooperative should therefore check whether the $0.75 premium is actually realised in orders before expanding certified graded timber, using the 350-decorator survey as a guide rather than a guarantee, and monitor whether certification adds more to cost than to price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using RTPL's survey, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in timber and transport input costs will affect RTPL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If the $240,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% of $240,000 = $1,800 (0.0075 x $240,000), which is small beside $280,000 fixed costs. If the loan is fixed, there is no immediate change. The higher rate may make the $400,000 share issue relatively more attractive for future funding and could slow renovation spending, which grew 3.1%, but the direct cash effect on RTPL is contained.

Minimum wage increase (4.8%, to $13.20 an hour): RTPL employs 36 members, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert does not give hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented and is not stated. The honest benchmark is productivity: 80,000 units divided by 36 workers is about 2,222 units per worker, so a wage rise is bearable only if productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $8.00 contribution narrows, hitting a cooperative already facing 14% labour turnover.

Timber and transport costs (11.2%): As an illustrative upper bound, if the full $12.00 variable cost rose 11.2%, that adds $1.34 a unit (0.112 x $12.00 = $1.344); at 80,000 units that is about $107,520 a year (80,000 x $1.344). Even partial pass-through materially cuts contribution, though the $0.75 certified-flooring premium and supplier negotiation can offset some of it.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in timber and transport input costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 80,000 units and directly threatens the $8.00 contribution that funds the $640,000 line, whereas the interest rise is about $1,800 and the wage effect can be managed through productivity. RTPL should focus on waste reduction and passing the certification premium through to decorators.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the external factors with minimal application to RTPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the impact of at least two of the three changes on RTPL's costs, revenue or financing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
